dedupe_keys.name: evacuation decision making in the 2016 chimney tops 2 fire gatlinburg tennessee nist household survey

description: This case study reports a household survey on emergency communication and evacuation decisions during the 2016 Chimney Tops 2 wildfire, which spread into residential areas of Gatlinburg, Tennessee. The National Institute of Standards and Technology produced it, through a small business survey research contractor, and published it as a government report in July 2020, free to read on GovInfo as a US government work. Homeowners in the Gatlinburg area answered an online survey from October 2018 to May 2019, and the final sample held 323 participants, with a thematic analysis of free-text comments. Coverage is the Gatlinburg area. Caveats: the sample is self-selected homeowners surveyed two to three years after the fire, responses rely on recall, and the survey microdata are not published with the report. The survey found most participants were largely unaware of wildfire risk and had not evacuated before; few received official information or evacuation notices, relying instead on media, social sources and cues from the fire itself; most evacuated on the day the fire reached residential areas, prompted by intense fire cues and fear; and many felt unprepared. The report recommends outreach on local wildfire risk and timely, coordinated, clear warnings and signage. Simulation uses: parameterising warning receipt and departure timing in wildfire evacuation and agent-based emergency response models. Related records: the Common Alerting Protocol (data-oasis-common-alerting-protocol-cap) standardises warnings and OpenFEMA (data-openfema) holds disaster declarations.
